subject: Medicine
summary: Tetanus is a life‑threatening neuroparalytic disease caused by Clostridium tetani toxin, usually from contaminated wounds. Rapid diagnosis, wound care, antitoxin and supportive care are essential.

sections.p: Tetanus is a toxin‑mediated disease where C. tetani releases tetanospasmin, causing sustained muscle contraction. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by history of wound and vaccination status.
b: Classic trismus, generalized spasm, risus sardonicus

t.b: Detects C. tetani; positive confirms source but not needed for treatment
Rarely used; positive confirms toxin presence but not required for management

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Modified Tetanus Severity Score (mTSS). It guides ICU need and predicts mortality.
The most common cause is a contaminated puncture or burn wound in an unvaccinated or partially vaccinated individual.
b: Traumatic puncture wounds, burns, surgical wounds, animal bites

sections.p: Early signs include trismus and jaw stiffness, progressing to generalized rigidity, spasms, and autonomic instability.
b: Trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, hyperthermia, tachycardia

sections.p: Investigations are supportive; focus on ruling out other causes of rigidity and assessing complications.

t.b: Rule out sepsis; leukocytosis may indicate infection
Identify hypocalcemia or hyponatremia that worsen spasms
Monitor for arrhythmias from autonomic dysfunction

sections.p: Complications can be fatal if not promptly managed. Watch for respiratory failure, autonomic instability, and sepsis.
b: Respiratory arrest, cardiac arrhythmia, aspiration pneumonia, sepsis

sections.p: Treat the source wound, give human tetanus immunoglobulin (HTIG) and tetanus toxoid, and provide supportive care in ICU.
b: Wound debridement, HTIG within 24h, tetanus toxoid booster, benzodiazepines for spasms, mechanical ventilation if needed

t.b: Neutralises circulating toxin; must be given within 24h of exposure
Reduce muscle tone and prevent autonomic crises
Used when airway is compromised or spasms are severe

sections.p: After recovery, complete the full tetanus toxoid series and counsel on wound care. Community vaccination remains key.
b: Complete DTP series, booster every 10 years, educate on clean wound care

sections.p: Conditions with muscle rigidity or spasms can mimic tetanus.
b: Myasthenia gravis, Guillain‑Barré syndrome, hypocalcemia, stroke

sections.p: Normal toxin assays do not exclude tetanus; clinical judgment prevails.
b: Negative culture or toxin assay does not rule out disease

whenToSeekHelp: Severe trismus, inability to swallow, respiratory distress, high fever, autonomic instability

faq.q: Can tetanus be prevented in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Yes, by ensuring timely tetanus toxoid vaccination and safe wound care.

faq.q: What is the role of antibiotics?
faq.a: They eradicate C. tetani but do not neutralise toxin; used alongside antitoxin.

faq.q: Is tetanus still common in developed countries?
faq.a: Rare, mainly in unvaccinated or partially vaccinated individuals.

exam: Describe the pathophysiology of tetanus toxin and its clinical consequences.
Explain the rationale for giving human tetanus immunoglobulin and tetanus toxoid in a patient with a contaminated wound.
Outline the management steps for a patient presenting with generalized muscle spasms and autonomic instability.
related: Public health strategies for vaccine-preventable diseases
